# Step-by-step guide to building Production-Ready Edge AI on nRF52840 with Zephyr RTOS and Edge Impulse

Edge AI is transforming embedded systems, enabling devices to sense, learn, and respond locally without cloud dependency. This comprehensive technical guide demonstrates how to build a complete Edge AI pipeline from data collection to on-device deployment using Zephyr RTOS, Edge Impulse, and the nRF52840 development kit.

## **What You'll Build**

By the end of this guide, you'll have working implementations for:

* **Continuous Motion Recognition** \- Classify walking, tilt, idle, and shake movements in real-time  
* **Sound Classification** \- Distinguish between noise, speech, and specific events  
* **Keyword Spotting** \- Recognize voice commands (yes/no/start/stop)

All running entirely on-device with sub-30ms inference latency and minimal power consumption.

## **Introduction**

The convergence of tiny machine learning (TinyML) and real-time operating systems has made Edge AI practical for production IoT applications. This tutorial demonstrates the complete workflow using:

* **Zephyr RTOS** \- A scalable, production-ready RTOS with comprehensive sensor support  
* **Edge Impulse** \- An end-to-end platform for embedded ML development  
* **nRF52840 DK** or **STM32 B-L475E-IOT01A** \- Industry-standard development boards

### **Why Edge AI Matters**

Traditional cloud-based ML approaches face critical limitations:

* **Latency**: Round-trip delays of 100-500ms make real-time applications impossible  
* **Privacy**: Sensitive sensor data leaves the device  
* **Connectivity**: Requires constant internet access  
* **Cost**: Cloud API fees scale with usage  
* **Bandwidth**: Streaming raw sensor data consumes significant bandwidth

Edge AI solves these problems by running inference locally:

* **Latency**: \<30ms for typical models  
* **Privacy**: All processing happens on-device  
* **Offline Operation**: No internet required  
* **Zero Cloud Costs**: One-time deployment  
* **Low Bandwidth**: Only transmit predictions, not raw data

## **Hardware Requirements**

### **Option 1: nRF52840 DK \+ External Sensor Shield**

**Development Board:** Nordic Semiconductor nRF52840 DK

* **MCU**: ARM Cortex-M4F @ 64 MHz  
* **Flash**: 1 MB  
* **RAM**: 256 KB  
* **Connectivity**: Bluetooth 5.0 LE, NFC  
* **Interfaces**: USB, UART, SPI, I2C, GPIO

**Sensor Shield:** X-NUCLEO-IKS01A3

* **LSM6DSO**: 6-axis IMU (accelerometer \+ gyroscope)  
* **LIS2MDL**: 3-axis magnetometer  
* **LIS2DW12**: Low-power 3-axis accelerometer  
* **HTS221**: Humidity and temperature sensor  
* **LPS22HH**: Pressure sensor

### **Option 2: STM32 B-L475E-IOT01A**

**Development Board:** STMicroelectronics B-L475E-IOT01A Discovery Kit

* **MCU**: ARM Cortex-M4F @ 80 MHz  
* **Flash**: 1 MB  
* **RAM**: 128 KB  
* **Connectivity**: WiFi, Bluetooth LE, NFC, Sub-GHz  
* **Built-in Sensors:**  
  * **LSM6DSL**: 6-axis IMU  
  * **LIS3MDL**: 3-axis magnetometer  
  * **HTS221**: Humidity and temperature  
  * **LPS22HB**: Pressure sensor  
  * **MP34DT01**: Digital MEMS microphone

### **Hardware Setup**

#### **nRF52840 DK Assembly**

1. Align X-NUCLEO-IKS01A3 shield with Arduino headers  
2. Carefully press the shield onto the headers. Ensure the shield doesn't touch the center pins  
3. Connect micro-USB cable to the SHORT side of the board  
4. Set power switch to ON  
5. Verify JLINK drive appears in your file system

#### **STM32 Setup**

1. Connect micro-USB cable  
2. Board mounts as DIS\_L4IOT drive  
3. All sensors are ready to use immediately

## **Software Stack Setup**

### **Prerequisites Installation**

#### **1\. Install Node.js 22 LTS**

**Linux/Ubuntu:**

\`\`\`bash  
curl \-sL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup\_22.x | sudo \-E bash \-  
sudo apt-get install \-y nodejs  
node \-v  \# Verify: v22.x or higher  
\`\`\`

#### **2\. Install Zephyr RTOS**

Zephyr RTOS Version: v4.4.0

Follow the official guide: [Zephyr Getting Started](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/develop/getting_started/)

Update the `west.yml` of your Zephyr repo adding the lines below for the SDK then call `west update` to download the SDK into your Zephyr repo.

Here are the lines to add the Edge Impulse SDK:

\`\`\`yaml  
   \- name: edge-impulse-sdk-zephyr  
      path: modules/edge-impulse-sdk-zephyr  
      revision: ${EI\_SDK\_VERSION}  
      url: [https://github.com/edgeimpulse/edge-impulse-sdk-zephyr](https://github.com/edgeimpulse/edge-impulse-sdk-zephyr)  
\`\`\`

#### **3\. Install Edge Impulse CLI**

\`\`\`bash  
npm install \-g edge-impulse-cli \--force

\# Verify installation  
edge-impulse-daemon \--version  
edge-impulse-data-forwarder \--version  
edge-impulse-run-impulse \--version  
\`\`\`

#### **4\. Create Edge Impulse Account**

1. Visit [Edge Impulse Studio](https://studio.edgeimpulse.com/signup)  
2. Sign up for a free account  
3. Create a new project (e.g., "nRF52840-Motion-Recognition")

## **Data Collection with Data Forwarder**

### **Understanding the Data Forwarder**

The Data Forwarder is a Zephyr application that streams sensor data to Edge Impulse via serial connection. It handles:

* Real-time sensor sampling at precise frequencies  
* Data formatting (CSV/tab-delimited)  
* Serial transmission  
* Automatic frequency detection by Edge Impulse CLI

### **Data Forwarder Implementation**

**Project Structure:**

\`\`\`bash  
data\_forwarder/  
├── src/main.cpp  
├── boards/  
│   ├── nrf52840dk\_nrf52840.conf  
│   └── disco\_l475\_iot1.conf  
├── CMakeLists.txt  
└── prj.conf  
\`\`\`

### **Building and Flashing**

\`\`\`bash  
cd data\_forwarder  
\# Build for nRF52840 DK  
west build \-p \-b nrf52840dk/nrf52840  
west flash  
\# or  
west flash \-r jlink  
\# Build for STM32 B-L475E-IOT01A  
west build \-p \-b disco\_l475\_iot01  
west flash  
\`\`\`

### **Data Collection Workflow**

**1\. Connect Device to Edge Impulse:**

\`\`\`bash  
edge-impulse-data-forwarder  
\# Follow prompts:  
\# \- Login credentials  
\# \- Project selection  
\# \- Axes naming: accX, accY, accZ  
\# \- Device name  
\`\`\`

Example output:  
\`\`\`bash  
Edge Impulse data forwarder v1.37.3  
? What is your user name or e-mail address (edgeimpulse.com)? \<your e-mail address\>  
? What is your password? \[hidden\]  
Endpoints:  
    Websocket: wss://remote-mgmt.edgeimpulse.com  
    API:       https://studio.edgeimpulse.com  
    Ingestion: https://ingestion.edgeimpulse.com

\[SER\] Connecting to /dev/ttyACM0  
\[SER\] Serial is connected (00:06:83:94:40:08)  
\[WS \] Connecting to wss://remote-mgmt.edgeimpulse.com  
\[WS \] Connected to wss://remote-mgmt.edgeimpulse.com

\[SER\] Detecting data frequency...  
\[SER\] Detected data frequency: 102Hz  
? 3 sensor axes detected (example values: \[-0.431,-0.134,9.418\]). What do you want to call them? Separate the names with ',': accX,accY,accZ  
\[WS \] Device "test\_device" is now connected to project "AnkyXCoder-project-1". To connect to another project, run \`edge-impulse-data-forwarder \--clean\`.  
\[WS \] Go to https://studio.edgeimpulse.com/studio/123064/acquisition/training to build your machine learning model\!  
\`\`\`

**2\. Collect Training Data:**

In Edge Impulse Studio → Data Acquisition:

* Set label (e.g., "square")  
* Sample length: 10000 ms  
* Click "Start sampling"  
* Perform continuous motion for 10 seconds  
* Repeat 10-15 times per class

![][image2]

**Best Practices:**

* Collect 3+ minutes per class  
* Vary speed (slow/fast movements)  
* Test different orientations  
* Include edge cases  
* Maintain continuous motion during recording  
* Balanced dataset (equal samples per class)

## **Building Machine Learning Models**

### **Continuous Motion Recognition**

#### **Step 1: Create Impulse**

In Edge Impulse Studio → Create Impulse:

**Configuration:**

* Window size: `2000 ms` (2-second sliding window)  
* Window increase: `80 ms` (sliding step)  
* Frequency: `62.5 Hz` (sampling rate)

**Blocks:**

1. **Processing Block**: Spectral Analysis  
2. **Learning Block**: Classification

Click **Save Impulse**.

![][image3]

#### **Step 2: Configure Spectral Features**

Navigate to **Spectral features**:

**Filter Configuration:**

* Filter type: Low-pass  
* Cutoff frequency: 3 Hz  
* Filter order: 6

**Rationale**: Low-pass filter removes high-frequency noise while preserving motion patterns (typically \<3 Hz for human movement).

![][image4]

Click **Save parameters** → **Generate features**.

**Expected Result**: Feature Explorer shows distinct clusters for each class.

![][image5]

#### **Step 3: Train Neural Network**

Navigate to **NN Classifier**:

**Architecture**:

Input layer: 39 features (from spectral analysis)

Dense layer: 20 neurons, ReLU activation

Dense layer: 20 neurons, ReLU activation

Output layer: 4 neurons (number of classes)

**Training Configuration:**

* Learning rate: 0.0005  
* Training cycles (epochs): 30  
* Validation set: 20%  
* Auto-balance dataset: Enabled

Click **Start training**.

![][image6]

**Target Metrics:**

* Training accuracy: \>95%  
* Validation accuracy: \>90%  
* Loss: \<0.3

**If accuracy is low:**

* Collect more diverse data  
* Increase epochs to 50-100  
* Adjust learning rate  
* Try different architectures

#### **Step 4: Anomaly Detection**

In Edge Impulse Studio → Create Impulse:

**Blocks:**

1. **Learning Block**: Anomaly Detection

Click **Save Impulse**.

#### **![][image7]**

#### **Step 5: Anomaly Detection**

Navigate to **Anomaly Detection Settings**.

* number of components: `32`  
* Click on the **Select suggested axes** button to harness the results of the [feature importance](https://docs.edgeimpulse.com/studio/projects/processing-blocks#feature-importance) output.  
* Select accX RMS, accY RMS and accZ RMS axes.

Click **Save & train** to generate the clusters.

![][image8]

#### **Step 6: Model Testing**

Navigate to **Model testing** → **Classify all**.

![][image9]

**Expected Performance:**

* Overall accuracy: \>85%  
* Per-class accuracy: \>80%  
* Confusion matrix: Clear diagonal

## **On-Device Inference Implementation**

### **Building and Deploying the Model**

**1\. Build Edge Impulse Model:**

**Use `west ei-build` to trigger a new build of your Edge Impulse model deployment in Studio:**

**\# Build the latest model configuration from your Edge Impulse project**

**west ei-build \-k ei\_abc123... \-p 12345**

**\# With optional parameters**

**west ei-build \-k ei\_abc123... \-p 12345 \-e tflite-eon \-t int8 \-i 1**

**![][image10]**

**![][image11]**

**Required arguments:**

* **`-k, --api-key` \- Your Edge Impulse API key**  
* **`-p, --project` \- Your Edge Impulse project ID (integer)**

**Optional arguments:**

* **`-i, --impulseid` \- Specific impulse ID to build (default: 1\)**  
* **`-e, --engine` \- Build engine: `tflite` or `tflite-eon` (default: `tflite-eon`)**  
* **`-t, --modeltype` \- Model type: `int8` or `float32` (default: `int8`)**

**This command:**

* **Calls the Edge Impulse [Build On-Device Model API](https://docs.edgeimpulse.com/apis/studio/jobs/build-on-device-model)**  
* **Triggers a fresh build of your Zephyr library deployment in Studio**  
* **Waits for the build to complete**  
* **Useful when you’ve made changes to your impulse configuration**

**2\. Download Edge Impulse Model:**

#### **`west ei-deploy` \- Download deployment artifacts**

**Use `west ei-deploy` to download your pre-built Edge Impulse model deployment:**

**\# Download the latest built model from your Edge Impulse project**

**west ei-deploy \-k ei\_abc123... \-p 12345**

**\# With optional parameters**

**west ei-deploy \-k ei\_abc123... \-p 12345 \-e tflite-eon \-t int8 \-i 1**

**\# The zip file is downloaded as ei\_model.zip**

**\# Extract it to the model/ directory**

**unzip ei\_model.zip \-d ./model**

**Required arguments:**

* **`-k, --api-key` \- Your Edge Impulse API key**  
* **`-p, --project` \- Your Edge Impulse project ID (integer)**

**Optional arguments:**

* **`-i, --impulseid` \- Specific impulse ID to download (default: 1\)**  
* **`-e, --engine` \- Build engine: `tflite` or `tflite-eon` (default: `tflite-eon`)**  
* **`-t, --modeltype` \- Model type: `int8` or `float32` (default: `int8`)**

**This command:**

* **Calls the Edge Impulse [Download Deployment API](https://docs.edgeimpulse.com/apis/studio/deployment/download)**  
* **Downloads the latest Zephyr library deployment as `ei_model.zip`**  
* **You must manually extract it to the `model/` directory**

**unzip ei\_model.zip \-d ./model**

### **Inference Application Implementation**

**Project Structure:**

\`\`\`bash  
inference\_app/  
├── src/main.cpp  
├── model/  \# Extracted model  
├── boards/  
│   ├── nrf52840dk\_nrf52840.conf  
│   └── disco\_l475\_iot1.conf  
├── CMakeLists.txt  
└── prj.conf  
\`\`\`

### **Building and Flashing**

\`\`\`bash  
cd inference\_app  
\# Build for nRF52840 DK  
west build \-p \-b nrf52840dk/nrf52840  
west flash  
\# or  
west flash \-r jlink  
\# Build for STM32 B-L475E-IOT01A  
west build \-p \-b disco\_l475\_iot01  
west flash  
\`\`\`

\`\`\`bash  
\=== Edge Impulse Inference \===  
Model: motion-recognition  
Classes: 4  
Window: 2000 ms

Starting inference…

Timing: DSP=17 ms, NN=8 ms

## **Performance Optimization**

### **Hardware Acceleration**

**ARM CMSIS-NN** provides optimized kernels for:

* Convolution layers  
* Fully connected layers  
* Pooling operations  
* Activation functions

**Enable in CMakeLists.txt:**

\`\`\`cmake  
\# Edge Impulse / CMSIS-NN flags (apply to app instead of unknown target)  
add\_definitions(-DEIDSP\_USE\_CMSIS\_DSP=1  
               \-DEIDSP\_LOAD\_CMSIS\_DSP\_SOURCES=1  
               \-DEI\_CLASSIFIER\_TFLITE\_ENABLE\_CMSIS\_NN=1  
               \-DARM\_MATH\_LOOPUNROLL)  
\`\`\`

**Performance Improvement:**

* 2-4x faster inference  
* 30-50% lower power consumption

### **Model Quantization**

**int8 Quantization** reduces model size and speeds up inference:

In Edge Impulse → EON Tuner:

* Enable int8 quantization  
* Calibrate with representative dataset  
* Rebuild model

**Benefits:**

* 4x smaller model size (Flash savings)  
* 2-3x faster inference  
* \<2% accuracy loss typically

**Results:**

Before quantization:  
\- Model size: 112 KB  
\- Inference: 25 ms  
\- RAM: 35 KB

After int8 quantization:  
\- Model size: 28 KB  
\- Inference: 12 ms  
\- RAM: 20 KB

### **Key Takeaways**

1. **Zephyr RTOS** provides a robust foundation for Edge AI with comprehensive driver support and power management  
2. **Edge Impulse** dramatically accelerates ML development from weeks to days  
3. **On-device inference** enables privacy-preserving, low-latency applications  
4. **Hardware acceleration** (CMSIS-NN) and quantization make TinyML practical on constrained devices  
5. **Production deployment** requires careful attention to power, memory, and fault tolerance
